topic: Breakthrough Starshot: the plan to reach another star in 20 years, and why it stalled
title: The $100 Million Plan to Reach Another Star (And Why It Stalled)
title_variants: We Almost Sent a Probe to Alpha Centauri
Humanity's Real Plan to Visit Another Star in 20 Years
description:
In 2016, Yuri Milner and Stephen Hawking announced Breakthrough Starshot: gram-scale probes riding laser-pushed light sails to Alpha Centauri at up to a fifth of the speed of light, arriving in about 20 years.

This video walks through how it was supposed to work, the physics problems that stood in the way, and why, in 2025, the project's own director said it had been put on hold.

Sources: Breakthrough Initiatives; ESO press release eso1629 (Proxima b); Scientific American, "The Quiet Demise of Breakthrough Starshot" (Sept 2025); Hoang et al. and Loeb on interstellar dust.
comment_question: If a probe launched today and sent back photos of Proxima b in 2050, would you still be watching? What would you want it to look for first?

scenes.narration: Imagine a spacecraft lighter than a paperclip, riding a beam of light so powerful it reaches a fifth of the speed of light in minutes. Twenty years later, it flies past a planet orbiting another star. This wasn't a movie pitch. In 2016, it was a real plan, with real money behind it. So what happened?

visual.prompt: a tiny glowing light sail spacecraft streaking away from Earth on a brilliant laser beam, Earth in the lower corner, stars ahead

scenes.narration: On the twelfth of April, 2016, in New York, the investor Yuri Milner stood on stage with Stephen Hawking and announced Breakthrough Starshot. Milner pledged one hundred million dollars, not to launch anything, but to find out whether it could be done at all. Mark Zuckerberg joined Hawking on the board.

visual.prompt: a press conference stage with a starfield backdrop

scenes.narration: The target was Alpha Centauri, the closest star system to the Sun, about four point three seven light years away. That sounds close, until you do the maths. Voyager 1, one of the fastest objects we've ever sent out of the solar system, moves at about seventeen kilometres per second. At that pace, crossing that distance would take more than seventy thousand years.

visual.prompt: the Alpha Centauri triple star system, two bright yellow-orange suns and a small distant red dwarf, deep space

scenes.narration: Starshot wanted to do it within a single human career. The idea was to cut the travel time from tens of thousands of years to around twenty. To get there, the team had to throw out almost everything we know about building spacecraft, starting with the idea that a spacecraft should carry its own fuel.

Four months after the announcement, the mission got a destination. On the twenty-fourth of August, 2016, the European Southern Observatory announced a planet orbiting Proxima Centauri, the small red dwarf in the Alpha Centauri system, and the nearest star to us of all. They called it Proxima b.

Proxima b circles its star every eleven point two days, and it has at least roughly the mass of Earth. Crucially, it sits in the habitable zone, the band of orbits where temperatures could allow liquid water on the surface. Whether it actually has an atmosphere, let alone water, is still unknown.

visual.prompt: a rocky exoplanet orbiting close to a dim red dwarf star, the planet's dayside lit deep red, a thin hint of atmosphere at the limb

scenes.narration: That uncertainty is exactly why people wanted to go. Proxima is a flare star, prone to violent outbursts of radiation that could strip a planet bare. From here, we can only measure the planet indirectly. A probe passing close by could, in principle, send back the first close-up look at a world around another star.

visual.prompt: a red dwarf star erupting in a massive stellar flare, arcs of plasma, a small planet silhouetted in the foreground

scenes.narration: Here's the core trick. Instead of a rocket, Starshot would use a light sail. Light carries momentum, and when it reflects off a mirror it gives that mirror a tiny push. Sunlight alone has already sailed spacecraft. Japan's IKAROS unfurled a solar sail on its way to Venus in 2010, and the Planetary Society's LightSail 2 raised its own orbit with sunlight in 2019.

visual.prompt: a large square reflective solar sail unfurled in space, sunlight glinting across its surface, planet below

scenes.narration: But sunlight is gentle. To reach a fifth of light speed, Starshot planned to replace the Sun with lasers: an array of them on the ground, spread over roughly a square kilometre, firing together with a combined output of up to one hundred gigawatts. That's in the range of the output of many large power stations combined, focused onto one tiny target.

visual.prompt: a vast array of thousands of laser emitters on a high desert plateau at night, beams converging into a single brilliant column into the sky

scenes.narration: The spacecraft itself would be almost nothing. A sail about four metres across, and a chip weighing just a few grams, carrying a camera, sensors, power and a way to talk home. The team called it a StarChip. Because each one would be so cheap, the plan was to launch many of them, accepting that a lot would fail.

visual.prompt: close-up macro of a gram-scale spacecraft chip at the centre of an ultra-thin shimmering square sail, circuitry visible, studio-like lighting in space

scenes.narration: Why does everything have to be so small? Because of energy. The energy of motion grows with mass, and with the square of speed. At a fifth of the speed of light, a single gram carries about as much energy as four hundred tonnes of TNT. Every extra gram means more laser power, so the probe has to be almost weightless. That's not a design choice. It's what the physics demands.

visual.prompt: a single glowing gram-sized probe beside a towering abstract column of energy, visual metaphor for immense kinetic energy, dark space background

scenes.narration: Then the laser fires. For about ten minutes, the sail would be hit with so much light that it would accelerate at thousands of times the force of Earth's gravity. Estimates run from around ten thousand g to forty thousand g. By the time the beam shut off, the probe would already be leaving the solar system at tens of thousands of kilometres every second.

At fifteen to twenty percent of the speed of light, the trip takes roughly twenty to thirty years. There'd be no braking. The probes would simply scream past the Alpha Centauri system, snapping what they could in a matter of hours. Then the data still has to make its way home, which takes another four years or so, travelling at the speed of light.

visual.prompt: a tiny probe streaking past a red dwarf star and its planet at incredible speed, motion trail of light, cinematic

scenes.narration: On paper, the physics worked. Nothing in the plan broke the laws of nature. The problem was engineering, and the list of hard problems was long. The first was the laser itself. No single laser could ever do this, so you'd need millions of smaller ones working together, their light waves lined up precisely in step.

And between the lasers and space sits our atmosphere, constantly churning. Turbulence bends and smears a beam. Keeping it focused on a sail would need millions of corrections every second. Starshot's own leaders described that as possibly the single largest hurdle. Then there's price: laser power would need to fall from around a hundred dollars per watt to just a few cents.

The sail is its own nightmare. It has to be big, almost weightless, and so reflective that it doesn't simply vaporise under a beam strong enough to light a city. It also has to stay stable. Push unevenly on a thin sheet and it twists, wobbles, or tumbles out of the beam. Researchers have made promising materials, like silicon nitride, but so far only at millimetre scales, not metres.

visual.prompt: an ultra-thin reflective sail glowing white-hot at its edges under an intense laser, rippling slightly, dramatic

scenes.narration: Then there's the journey itself. Space between the stars isn't empty. It's thinly scattered with gas and dust. At a fifth of light speed, even a speck of dust hits with the energy of an explosive. One analysis estimated that dust could erode up to thirty percent of a probe's surface on the way, unless it carried a few millimetres of shielding.

And if a probe did survive, how would it phone home? A device weighing a few grams has very little power, and it would be more than four light years away. Picking up that whisper of a signal would take enormous receiving telescopes back on Earth. One researcher called communication the elephant in the room.

There was also a problem that has nothing to do with physics. A laser array powerful enough to launch a starship is, uncomfortably, also a very powerful weapon. Building one would need a level of international trust and cooperation that, honestly, we haven't had much practice at.

visual.prompt: a world map at night with glowing lines connecting nations to a single laser facility, tense, strategic atmosphere

scenes.narration: So what happened? There was never a dramatic cancellation. In September 2025, Scientific American reported that funding had dried up and meetings had stopped. Pete Worden, Starshot's executive director, said in an email that they had put the program on hold and were working to transition portions of it to others.

visual.prompt: an empty mission control room with dimmed screens still showing a star map of Alpha Centauri, dust in the light, melancholy

scenes.narration: And that hundred million dollars? According to an estimate by physicist Philip Lubin, whose lab received Starshot grants, only around four and a half million was actually spent, across roughly thirty contracts. Against Milner's own estimate that a real mission would cost five to ten billion dollars, the project never got close to the money it would truly need.

But calling Starshot a failure misses something. It did what its first hundred million was meant to do: it took a science-fiction idea seriously enough to find where the real walls are. Researchers it funded worked on sail materials, laser physics and beam stability, problems that might otherwise never have been studied.

Some of the work goes on. Zachary Manchester's tiny ChipSats, which received small amounts of Breakthrough funding, flew in orbit, with over a hundred deployed in 2019. And the core idea, using light rather than fuel to push very small spacecraft, keeps appearing in new research and mission concepts.

visual.prompt: a swarm of hundreds of tiny postage-stamp sized satellites drifting in low Earth orbit, glinting in sunlight, Earth curve below

scenes.narration: So, could we still do it? The honest answer is: not with today's technology, and not with today's budgets. Lasers need to become dramatically cheaper. Sails need to scale up a thousand times. And we need a way to hear a whisper from four light years away. None of those are forbidden by physics. They're just very, very hard.

visual.prompt: a lone figure on a hilltop at night looking up at the bright stars of Alpha Centauri low on the southern horizon, Milky Way overhead

scenes.narration: Starshot showed us something important, though. Reaching another star isn't a question of if the laws of nature allow it. They do. It's a question of whether we decide it's worth the effort, together. Every generation gets to answer that for itself.

If a probe launched in your lifetime and sent back the first picture of Proxima b, what would you hope to see? Tell me in the comments. And if you want more real science behind the sci-fi, subscribe, because next time we're looking at what it would actually take to slow down when you get there.

visual.prompt: the first imagined close-up photograph of a rocky red-lit exoplanet taken by a passing probe, slight motion blur, grainy, awe-inspiring
